theme: Premises and the physics of the room
howNumbersWereChecked: November 14, 2026, two passes. First pass: the session could search the web but could not open pages. Second pass, after the session was given network access to city and federal sites: I downloaded and read the primary documents myself (Health Code Article 81 and Chapter 23, the 2022 Building and Plumbing Codes, the Buildings penalty schedule 1 RCNY 102-01, the Dining Out NYC fee and enforcement pages, NYC311 articles, DEP, FDNY, DCWP, Landmarks, the Water Board rate schedule, IRS Form 8826, the Access Board guide, NYC Open Data). Every record marked 'verified' says how: "checkedVia": "page_opened" = I opened the primary source and saw the number; "checkedVia": "search_excerpt" = the number was shown by the search tool in an excerpt of the primary source, but the page itself was not reachable (press sites, retailers, the online code library, which answered 403). 'estimate' = secondary sources (contractor and vendor guides, press), the research notes, memory (always said so in the note) or my own arithmetic, with the calculation in the note. Effects of levers and events (demand, quality, seat turns) are game-balance values unless the note cites a study.

sizing.note: Revised by D02. sqftPerUnit 18 -> 21: the engine divides 60% of the floor by this number, and 18 put 26 seats into 800 sq ft, above the research notes' own 15-25. Floor budget for 800 sq ft (extra.floorPlan): service bar 120, queue and pickup 70, accessible restroom 60, back of house 120, entry 25 = 395 sq ft that never holds a chair; 405 sq ft is left for seating; at 18 net sq ft per seat that is 22 seats, and 480 / 22 = 21. Anchors: the 2022 NYC Building Code counts 15 net sq ft per person at tables and chairs, 5 net sq ft per standing person and 200 gross sq ft per person in a commercial kitchen (Table 1004.1.3, read in the city's own PDF); vendor seating charts give 11-14 sq ft per seat for fast food, 12-15 full service, 18-20 fine dining; a Russian planning guide gives 1.6 sq m (17 sq ft) per guest. unitsServedPerSizeMonth stays 170, now with a derivation: 12 open hours, mean seat occupancy 47%, mean stay 60 minutes (70% short stays of 35 minutes, 30% laptop stays of 120 minutes) = 5.6 seated orders per seat a day. Stay lengths: Bloom Intelligence Wi-Fi data, 25 US coffee shops, June-September 2026: 32 minutes for a one-time visitor, almost two hours for the most frequent ones. takeawayShare stays 0.6: no public to-go split exists for independent cafes; the National Restaurant Association puts off-premises at nearly 75% of all restaurant traffic, drive-thru included. crowdPenaltyAbove 0.9 -> 0.85: solo guests hold two-tops, so a room is full when well under all chairs are taken (see extra.mechanics effective_seats_and_table_mix). emptyPenaltyBelow 0.4 -> 0.3: evidence that an empty room repels coffee buyers is weak (one 2025 survey study on crowding as social proof), so the penalty should start later. Both thresholds stay game-balance values.

setup.name: Customer restroom upgrade (needed for 20 or more seats)
setup.agency: NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (DOHMH)
setup.note: Same id as in the pack; the price stays the earlier allowance (no public NYC price was found), the rule is now exact and was read in the Health Code itself. Section 81.22(b): food service establishments with a seating capacity of 20 or more shall provide toilet facilities for patrons, except premises where a permitted food service establishment operated on or before December 5, 1977; such premises must add patron toilets when a renovation needs a Department of Buildings construction permit. 81.22(d): patrons and staff may share a toilet unless patrons would have to walk through a kitchen, food preparation or storage area or utensil washing area. NYC Health counts indoor and outdoor seats together. The Plumbing Code (403.2, 403.3) adds a second step that bites when a space is built or altered: where customers must be given a toilet and the space holds more than 30 people, staff included, separate facilities are required, which two single all-gender toilet rooms satisfy; the toilets may be one story up or down. The U.S. Access Board sets no minimum room size. A one-person toilet room must carry an all-gender sign (Local Law 79 of 2016).

setup.name: Portable threshold ramp for a one-step entrance
setup.note: Retailer listing seen in a search excerpt (the shop's site could not be opened): AlumiRamp aluminum threshold ramp $112.99 for a 6-inch rise, $156.99 for a 12-inch rise. A stopgap, not a compliant ramp: the Buildings Department's storefront guide gives a maximum slope of 1:12, a clear width of at least 36 inches and a 60-inch landing, so a 7-inch step needs 7 feet of ramp. Building Code 3202.2.2.1: for a building put up before December 6, 1969 a wheelchair ramp may, with the Buildings Commissioner's approval, project up to 44 inches past the street line; anything further needs the Transportation Department. No public price for a permanent storefront ramp in NYC was found.

setup.name: Automatic door opener with push plate
setup.note: Vendor guides: a low-energy swing door operator runs $2,000-$5,000 installed nationally; one New York / New Jersey installer puts most complete openings at $7,500-$15,000. $5,000 is the top of the national range, taken as the low end for NYC. Not required by law for an existing door that a wheelchair user can open.

setup.name: Dedicated 208-240V circuit for the espresso machine
setup.note: Vendor guides: a two-group machine wants its own 30-amp circuit at 208-240V, a three-group machine about 40 amps; each grinder needs a separate 110V circuit. Adding one 220V circuit costs $500-$2,000 depending on the panel and the distance (vendor ballpark, not an NYC quote); $1,250 is the midpoint. Already present in a former cafe.

setup.name: Electrical service upgrade to 200 amps
setup.agency: Con Edison; NYC Department of Buildings (electrical permit)
setup.note: Needed when the panel cannot carry the bar: a two-group espresso machine (30 A), dishwasher, ice machine, fridges and air conditioning together. Price: a directory page gives $5,500-$10,000 for a 200-amp panel upgrade in NYC, a national guide $5,000-$15,000 for small commercial three-phase service; $8,000 is the middle. No official price exists. Wait: one NYC electrician quotes 4-12 weeks from the load letter, a 2026 guide 12-24 weeks (6-10 weeks for Con Edison layout drawings, 3-5 weeks of inspections); 84 days is the overlap. Rent runs the whole time.

setup.name: Backflow prevention device on the water line
setup.note: DEP backflow FAQ, read on the page: food preparation facilities are on the list of businesses that must install a backflow prevention device; DEP's own cost guide says installation should cost $3,000-$5,000 for a very small one-story building and $3,750-$5,500 for a small two-story one ($4,000 is the middle of the first band). A licensed master plumber installs it after a plan filed by an architect or engineer, the test report goes to DEP within 30 days, and the device must then be tested every 12 months by a certified tester; DEP mails a notice when the test is due, and failure can bring fines or disconnection of the water service. The device sits on the building's water service line: in a former cafe it is already there, and the lease decides who pays for the yearly test.

setup.name: Under-sink grease interceptor, installed
setup.note: DEP, read on the page: every business that disposes of grease should have a properly sized grease interceptor (15 RCNY 19-11); food waste grinders are not allowed in NYC commercial establishments. Price: national cost guides put an indoor under-sink unit at $500-$3,000 installed and add 30%-50% for labor in New York; $2,500 is my figure inside that band. DEP requires that only licensed plumbers install grease interceptors, and its inspectors order an undersized unit replaced. A former cafe has one; a former shop or salon does not, and the build-out price for such a space should already include it.

setup.name: Replace the air conditioning unit
setup.note: NYC contractor pages: small commercial split systems and rooftop units $8,000-$40,000; a 5-10 ton rooftop replacement with curb adapter and rigging $18,000-$45,000; a national guide puts 4-5 ton units at $9,000-$14,500 installed. An 800 sq ft cafe needs about 3-5 tons; $15,000 is my figure for one unit with rigging. Most small leases make the tenant pay for repair and replacement of the unit that serves the space: ask who owns it before signing. The 15-year life is a planning value.

setup.name: See-through roll-down security grille
setup.note: Gothamist, 2026: a bakery owner was quoted $6,000-$7,000 to replace one gate; other reports give $5,000-$20,000. Buildings Department service notice of February 17, 2026, read in full: under Local Law 75 of 2009 grilles on Group B and M storefronts had to give at least 70% visibility by July 1, 2026 (Administrative Code 28-315.7.1), landmark buildings and historic districts exempt; non-compliance is a major violation that can be cured within 90 days, and replacing a grille needs a registered design professional and a permit. Seen in search excerpts of the press and the Council record: on June 30, 2026 the City Council voted 51-0 (Int 0910-A) to drop the deadline, so the 70% rule now applies only when a grille is newly installed or replaced.

setup.name: Fabric storefront awning with the shop name
setup.note: Job costs declared on recent Buildings Department filings, read through a permit aggregator: a single storefront awning $2,000 in Sunset Park, $2,800 in the East Village, $2,600 in an Upper East Side landmark district; retractable ones run to $15,000. The awning is a permitted job. Zoning limits what it may say: lettering no taller than 12 inches, no more than 12 sq ft, name and address only (as summarized in a LISC storefront guide; the zoning text was not opened). The 8-year fabric life is a planning value.

setup.name: Seasonal entrance vestibule (storm enclosure)
setup.note: One NYC fabricator lists temporary vestibules at $4,500-$10,000 with seasonal installation and removal included (seen in a search excerpt); $4,500 is the low end for a single door. NYC311, read on the page: storm enclosures are allowed from November 15 through April 15, and the city takes complaints about ones that have no permit, stand more than 18 inches beyond the street line or are not removed after April 15. A fabricator cites a larger allowance of 25 sq ft for eating and drinking places (not checked against the Building Code). The cost returns every winter.

setup.name: Air curtain over the front door
setup.note: Cost guide: a 48-inch unheated unit with professional installation is about $1,450; the installed range for one entrance is $900-$4,000, a heated unit can double the price, and the Northeast runs 10%-25% higher. A trade magazine case (ACHR News) describes a restaurant that ended cold-draft complaints with one.

setup.name: Dining Out NYC roadway cafe license
setup.agency: NYC Department of Transportation (Dining Out NYC)
setup.note: Dining Out NYC fee table, read on the program's site: license $1,050 for the four-year term, refundable security deposit $2,500, public hearing notice $500-$900 (required for every roadway application) = $4,450 with the top hearing figure; on top comes the yearly revocable consent fee per sq ft. Wait: the program site says review can take six months; the law caps a roadway review at 85 days (City Council report, April 2025); the 2026 Charter Revision Commission report says roadway applications take three to five months: 120 days here. A seasonal roadway cafe runs April 1 to November 29 and must be removed by November 30; since 2026 a year-round roadway license exists at higher rates.

setup.name: Roadway cafe structure: barriers, platform, furniture
setup.note: Streetsblog, April 2025: a roadway setup can easily cost more than $35,000 with city fees, construction and insurance; rental companies quote about $20,000 a season; one owner spent just over $5,000 on a simple one. $20,000 is the rental-season figure used as a purchase price for a plain compliant setup. Until 2026 the structure had to be taken down and stored every winter. The program's own fee example uses a 160 sq ft roadway cafe.

setup.name: Place of Assembly Certificate of Operation (75 or more people)
setup.agency: NYC Department of Buildings; Fire Department (FDNY) annual permit
setup.note: Read at the Buildings Department and in the Fire Department's restaurant guide: a Place of Assembly Certificate of Operation is required where 75 or more people gather indoors (200 outdoors), and the Fire Department counts restaurant staff in the 75. After the certificate an annual Fire Department Place of Assembly permit follows; its fee is on a sliding scale by occupancy and re-inspections are billed at $210 an hour. The $235 ($200 filing + $35 processing) is from the Buildings guide dated 2013 and may be out of date. The 60 days are my allowance. The real cost of crossing 74 people is not this fee: a second exit, doors that swing outward, filed seating plans and certified fire safety staff.

setup.name: Temporary Place of Assembly certificate for one event
setup.note: NYC Business, read on the page: the fee is $250, plus $100 for every day the request is late; it must be filed at least 10 business days before the event (14 calendar days). The legal way to hold one open-mic night or launch party for 75 or more people in a room that is normally under the line.

setup.name: Landmarks permit for a storefront, sign or awning
setup.note: Applies only in a historic district or a landmark building. Landmarks Commission storefront page, read: any change to the exterior of a storefront needs a permit, including a new storefront, awnings, signs and lighting, a new paint color, and an unenclosed sidewalk cafe (which also needs the Transportation Department). The 21 days stand for the 10 to 15 business days a 2018 fact sheet gives for staff-level permits (seen in a search excerpt only). No fee was found, so the cost is 0; the price is the wait and the designer's drawings.

setup.name: Replace one storefront glass panel
setup.note: Glazier guides (not NYC): a fixed panel of about 4 x 6 feet costs $800-$1,500 installed, a storefront window $500-$3,000 by size and glass type; $1,150 is the midpoint for one panel. Emergency board-up is extra. Used by the break-in event; most leases make the tenant responsible for the glass.

monthlyCosts.name: Sidewalk cafe yearly fee to the city (120 sq ft)
monthlyCosts.note: Dining Out NYC fee table, read on the program's site: $6, $10, $18 or $31 per sq ft a year for a sidewalk cafe by sector, and the program's own example is a 120 sq ft cafe: $720 a year in sector 1 ($60 a month), $1,200 in sector 2, $2,160 in sector 3, $3,720 in sector 4 ($310 a month). The City Council report adds that the cheapest sector covers at least 80% of the city and the two dearest lie in Manhattan at or below 125th Street. 120 sq ft holds about 10 chairs at the density of the city's old sidewalk cafe licenses. Charge only while a sidewalk cafe is licensed.

monthlyCosts.name: Roadway cafe yearly fee to the city (160 sq ft, year-round)
monthlyCosts.note: Dining Out NYC fee table, read on the program's site: a year-round roadway cafe pays the sidewalk rates ($6, $10, $18, $31 per sq ft a year by sector), a seasonal one $5, $8, $14, $25. The program's example is a 160 sq ft roadway cafe: $800 a year seasonal in sector 1; year-round that is 160 x $6 = $960 = $80 a month, and 160 x $31 = $4,960 = $413 a month in sector 4. Streetsblog's 'nearly $10,000 a year' is for a setup of the maximum size. Charge only while a roadway cafe is licensed.

monthlyCosts.name: Yearly backflow device test
monthlyCosts.note: DEP requires a test by a certified tester every 12 months (read in the DEP FAQ). Testing companies charge $150-$350 per device; $250 / 12 = $21 a month. The pack's maintenance line already names the backflow test: do not add both.

monthlyCosts.name: Air conditioning service contract
monthlyCosts.note: Vendor guides: quarterly preventive maintenance on one rooftop unit costs $180-$350 a visit, or $500-$2,500 per unit a year; small retail plans $500-$1,200. $1,200 a year = $100 a month for one unit. Charged through the hvac_care lever, not as a fixed line.

monthlyCosts.name: Yearly use fee for an illuminated sign
monthlyCosts.note: From the research notes (Administrative Code Table 28-112.2, not opened by me): the yearly fee for an illuminated sign is $45 up to 30 sq ft and $70 for 30-50 sq ft; $45 / 12 = $3.75. Only if the shop has a lit sign.

monthlyCosts.name: Fire Department permit for a rooftop or ceiling-hung cooling unit
monthlyCosts.note: Fire Department Restaurant Fire Safety Guide, read: a permit is required to install and operate a refrigerating system that is mounted on or suspended from a roof or ceiling (or uses certain refrigerants); a system under five horsepower with a group A1 refrigerant that is not on the roof or ceiling is exempt. Cost of permit: $105 per compressor, renewed annually: $105 / 12 = $8.75 a month for one compressor. Only for shops whose air conditioning is a rooftop or ceiling-hung unit.

monthlyCosts.name: Fire Department open flame permit (candles on tables)
monthlyCosts.note: Fire Department Restaurant Fire Safety Guide, read: a permit is required to use open flames, tabletop candles included, in any place of public gathering, and every restaurant with an occupancy under 75 is one; the annual inspection fee for the open flame permit is $210: $210 / 12 = $17.50 a month. Only for shops that light candles.

levers.name: Laptops and Wi-Fi

options.label: Laptops welcome, free Wi-Fi all day
No laptops at lunch and on weekends
No Wi-Fi, outlets covered, screens off the tables

levers.note: seatTurnsMult multiplies sizing.unitsServedPerSizeMonth (new field, see extra.mechanics seat_camping_dwell_mix). Derivation: with 30% of seated guests staying 120 minutes and 70% staying 35, the mean stay is 60 minutes; removing the long stays at peak hours brings it to about 50 (x1.2 turns), removing them all day to about 43 (x1.4). Demand losses are my estimates: seated laptop guests are about 12% of all orders (40% seated x 30%), and a part of them goes elsewhere. A real owner's account (NPR, 2014): a bakery cafe that switched off Wi-Fi and then banned screens at lunch saw sales rise, because people had been walking in, finding no table and leaving.

levers.name: Seating layout

options.label: Two-tops about two feet apart (18 sq ft per seat)
Squeeze the tables together (15 sq ft per seat)
One communal table and a window bar
Sofas and armchairs (22 sq ft per seat)

levers.note: seatsFitMult multiplies how many seats the address holds (18 / 15 = 1.2; 18 / 22 = 0.82). Evidence for the quality loss: Cornell field study in a New York restaurant (Robson and Kimes, 2009): guests at tables 20 inches or less apart were less satisfied in almost every category and less likely to return, although they left sooner; a 2011 survey of more than 1,000 Americans found strong objection to tables 6 and 12 inches apart. Communal seating raises turns because a solo guest takes one chair instead of a table for two or four. Lounge numbers are my estimates.

levers.name: Line and pickup

options.label: One register, the line forms where it can
Marked line, menu readable from the door, separate pickup shelf
Order-ahead by phone with a pickup shelf

levers.note: Evidence: a supermarket deli study (Lu, Musalem, Olivares, Schilkrut, Management Science 2013) found that shoppers react to how long the line looks, not to how fast it moves, and that the effect on buying is strong and non-linear; the working paper put a moderately longer line on a par with a 5% price rise. So a line that looks short (hidden bend, people waiting at pickup instead of in the queue) loses fewer buyers. Order-ahead costs bar capacity: Starbucks said a mid-teens percent of its mobile orders went uncompleted in spring 2024 because bars could not keep up. The effect sizes and monthly costs are game values.

levers.name: Restroom access

options.label: Customers only: door code printed on the receipt
Open to anyone who asks
No public restroom (legal only under 20 seats)

levers.note: The law, read in both codes: under 20 seats a food business owes customers no restroom (Health Code 81.22(b); Plumbing Code 403.3, exception 1), and NYC311 adds that food businesses need not open their employee toilets to the public; at 20 or more it must provide one, free of charge. The engine should refuse staff_only at 20 or more seats or attach the violation no_patron_toilet. Starbucks ended its open-door restroom policy on January 27, 2025 and now requires a purchase (press, search excerpt). The $150 for extra paper, soap and cleaning is my estimate.

levers.name: Air conditioning and ventilation

options.label: Quarterly service contract
Call someone when it breaks

levers.note: Contract price: vendor guides give $500-$2,500 a year per rooftop unit; $1,200 a year here. Without service the unit fails when it works hardest: see extra.eventCatalog ac_fails_in_heat_wave and extra.mechanics deferred_building_maintenance.

levers.name: Front door in winter

options.label: Just the door
Air curtain over the door
Seasonal vestibule, November 15 to April 15

levers.note: The air curtain needs the setup item air_curtain ($1,450); $25 a month is my estimate for its electricity. The vestibule is $4,500 a season spread over 12 months. Without either, the seats nearest the door are lost on cold days: extra.eventCatalog winter_draft_at_the_door.

levers.name: Outdoor seats

options.label: No outdoor seats
Licensed sidewalk cafe, 120 sq ft (about 10 seats)
Licensed roadway cafe, 160 sq ft (about 14 seats), all year

levers.note: Needs the license first (setup sidewalk_cafe_license or roadway_cafe_license; without it the option is the existing shortcut sidewalk_tables). Sizes and fees are the program's own examples: a 120 sq ft sidewalk cafe pays $720 a year in sector 1 ($60 a month; $310 in sector 4), a 160 sq ft year-round roadway cafe $960 ($80 a month; $413 in sector 4). Seats: the city's old sidewalk cafe license records (324 licenses in NYC Open Data with both figures) average 11.4 sq ft per chair: 120 / 11.4 = 10 chairs, 160 / 11.4 = 14. Outdoor seats count toward the 20-seat restroom line. Nothing may be stored or prepared outside, no smoking or vaping there, and the pest control contract must cover the outdoor area (NYC Health). The demand lift and the months people really sit outside are my estimates.

levers.name: Music

options.label: Slow, quiet playlist
Faster playlist at peak hours

levers.note: Evidence: Milliman (Journal of Consumer Research, 1986) found restaurant guests stay longer under slow music with no change in food spending; a 2024 field experiment in a restaurant measured 80 minutes under slow music against 57 under fast, with no significant difference in the bill. The 10% either way for a cafe is my estimate. Licensing the music is a separate cost (see D08).

levers.name: Step at the entrance

options.label: Portable ramp, call bell and a sign at the door
Leave the step as it is

levers.note: Only for an address with a step at the door. The ramp is the setup item portable_entrance_ramp ($157). Federal law asks an existing business to remove barriers where that is readily achievable. IRS Form 8826, read: a business with gross receipts of $1 million or less or no more than 30 full-time employees gets a credit of 50% of its access spending between $250 and $10,250 a year, at most $5,000.

shortcuts.name: Add chairs past the 19-seat line without a customer restroom
shortcuts.what: A few more chairs lift seated sales by about 3%, and you skip a $12,000 restroom. With 20 or more seats, outdoor ones included, and no toilet for customers the Health Department writes a critical violation: $300 and 10 points at each inspection, and the fix is still owed.

shortcuts.name: Stop restocking and checking the restroom
shortcuts.what: Nobody checks the paper, the bin or the door closer during the shift: about $60 a month of supplies and time saved. A toilet not maintained or supplied costs $200 and 2 to 5 points at inspection.

shortcuts.name: Hang a big lit sign without a permit
shortcuts.what: You skip the licensed sign hanger and the Buildings Department filing: about $150 a month spread over the first year. One anonymous 311 call brings an inspector: work without a permit is $1,250, or $6,250 if you miss the hearing. In 2018 such calls tripled and hundreds of small shops were fined.

shortcuts.name: A-frame sign and a bench out on the sidewalk
shortcuts.what: A sign in the walking path and a bench at the curb catch about 1% more buyers. Anything more than 3 feet from your wall or taller than 5 feet is a sidewalk obstruction: $50 the first time, $100 each time after, $300 if you ignore the ticket.

shortcuts.name: Stack deliveries in the back hallway and at the rear door
shortcuts.what: No storage room, so milk crates and cup boxes live in the exit path: you save about $100 a month on off-site storage or a bigger space. A blocked exit is a Fire Department summons of about $950, more for a repeat.

shortcuts.name: Skip the yearly backflow test
shortcuts.what: The device on your water line must be tested by a certified tester every 12 months: about $250 a year. Skip it and the city can fine you or disconnect your water; a health inspector can cite the missing protection too.

shortcuts.name: Pack the room for open-mic nights
shortcuts.what: Eighty people in a room approved for fewer than 75 bring about 2% more sales a month. More people than the Certificate of Occupancy allows is an immediately hazardous violation: $2,500, or $12,500 if you miss the hearing, with no cure. The legal way is a $250 temporary permit filed 10 business days ahead.

shortcuts.name: Put customer tables in the cellar
shortcuts.what: The cellar is free space: tables down there add about 3% to sales. A cellar approved for storage is not approved for customers: occupancy contrary to the Certificate of Occupancy costs $1,250, or $6,250 if you miss the hearing, and the tables have to go.

shortcuts.name: Turn the music up for evening events under apartments
shortcuts.what: A loud room keeps an evening crowd: about 1% more sales. Music from a business may not pass 42 decibels inside a neighbor's home. The first violation is $2,000, cut to $0 only if you prove you fixed it.

shortcuts.name: Add tables beyond your licensed outdoor area
shortcuts.what: Two more tables past the line on your site plan add about 1% to sales in season. The first time the city sends a corrective action request and gives you 30 days; after that it is $200, then $500 each time, and repeat offenders can lose the license.

violations.name: No customer toilet with 20 or more seats
violations.law: NYC Health Code §81.22(b), §81.22(d); 24 RCNY Chapter 23, Appendix 23-C, code 05E
violations.note: Read in the city's Chapter 23: scoring code 5E, "Toilet facility not provided for employees or for patrons when required. Shared patron-employee toilet accessed through kitchen, food prep or storage area or utensil washing area": 10 points (28 at the worst condition level), no lower levels. Penalty schedule, code 05E, critical: 81.22(a), (b) and (d) each $300, $350 at the worst level. Ten points alone leave four before the A is lost. The fine repeats at every inspection until the toilet exists or the seats go back under 20.

violations.name: Restroom not maintained or supplied
violations.law: NYC Health Code §81.22(c); 24 RCNY Chapter 23, Appendix 23-C, code 10A
violations.note: Read in the city's Chapter 23: scoring code 10A, "Toilet facility not maintained or provided with toilet paper, waste receptacle or self-closing door": 2 to 5 points. Penalty schedule, code 10A, general: toilet facility not properly maintained $200, not properly supplied $200, toilet room not enclosed with a self-closing door $200, the same at every condition level.

violations.name: Ventilation missing or in disrepair
violations.law: NYC Health Code §81.19(c); 24 RCNY Chapter 23, Appendix 23-C, code 10D
violations.note: Read in the city's Chapter 23: scoring code 10D, mechanical or natural ventilation not provided, improperly installed, in disrepair or failing to prevent build-up of heat, steam, vapors, odors, smoke and fumes: 2 to 5 points; penalty schedule 81.19(c): $200 at every level. Health Code 81.19(c) requires mechanical ventilation in rooms where odors, vapors or fumes originate. The fine is small; the real cost of neglected air conditioning is the failure in a heat wave.

violations.name: Business sign installed without a permit
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §28-105.1; 1 RCNY §102-01 (Buildings penalty schedule)
violations.note: Read in the Buildings penalty schedule (1 RCNY 102-01, city PDF dated July 2026): work without a permit under 28-105.1, Class 2: standard penalty $1,250, $6,250 on default, curable within 60 days; an outdoor sign on a display structure without a permit is also $1,250. Read on the Buildings sign page: no permit is needed for a sign painted directly on the wall or for a wall sign of 6 sq ft or less; anything else needs a permit, and only a licensed sign hanger may hang a sign over 75 sq ft or 25 pounds. History: in 2018 anonymous 311 complaints tripled (1,046 against 310 in 2017) and owners faced fines reported at $6,000; Local Law 28 of 2019 froze violations for signs that existed on February 9, 2019 and ended the Buildings Department's own extra civil penalty for business signs under 150 sq ft.

violations.name: Sign, bench or goods blocking the sidewalk
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §16-118(2)(a); 16 RCNY §19-103 (Sanitation penalty schedule)
violations.note: Read in the Sanitation Department's adopted penalty rule (2021): Local Law 80 of 2021 set the penalties under 16-118(2)(a), sidewalk obstruction included, at $50 for a first violation and $100 for a second and for each later one; the default penalty is $300. NYC311, read: sandwich and A-frame signs must not extend more than 3 feet into the sidewalk from the building or be higher than 5 feet. Game formula: $50, then $100.

violations.name: Exit path blocked by storage
violations.law: NYC Fire Code Chapter 10 (means of egress to be kept clear); summons returnable to OATH
violations.note: No official Fire Department schedule was opened. A fire-protection company's 2026 summary of the schedule gives the egress category a standard first penalty of $950 ($475 if corrected in time, $1,000 at most) and $2,375 for a repeat within 18 months ($5,000 at most); other vendor guides give $500-$2,500. The Fire Code section number is cited from memory.

violations.name: Backflow device missing or not tested
violations.law: NYC Health Code §81.20(a); 24 RCNY Chapter 23, code 10B; 10 NYCRR §5-1.31; 15 RCNY §20-04
violations.note: Two agencies. DEP FAQ, read: the device must be tested every 12 months by a certified tester, and failure can bring fines or disconnection of the water service; DEP's own fine amount was not found (a testing company's site says $500 per device). Health Department, read in Chapter 23: code 10B, back-flow prevention device not provided where required: 2 to 5 points (28 at worst); potable water not protected from back-flow $100, and $0 the first time if you prove the fix. The $100 is the Health Department figure. A City Council bill (Int 0768-2026) would raise the DEP penalty for not installing a device to $1,000-$10,000; its status was not confirmed. The state and city rule numbers are cited from memory.

violations.name: More people inside than the Certificate of Occupancy allows
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §28-118.3.2, §28-117.1; NYC Building Code §303.1.2; 1 RCNY §102-01
violations.note: Read in the Buildings penalty schedule (1 RCNY 102-01, city PDF dated July 2026): occupancy contrary to that allowed by the Certificate of Occupancy (28-118.3.2), Class 1: standard $2,500, default $12,500, no cure and no stipulation. Operating a place of assembly without a current Certificate of Operation (28-117.1), Class 1: the same $2,500 and $12,500; operating one where the Certificate of Occupancy does not allow it: $5,000 and $25,000. Read in the 2022 Building Code: one exit may serve at most 74 people in business or assembly use, and doors must swing outward from a room of 75 or more.

violations.name: Customer seating in a cellar approved only for storage
violations.note: Read in the Buildings penalty schedule (1 RCNY 102-01, city PDF dated July 2026): occupancy contrary to the Certificate of Occupancy (28-118.3.2), Class 2: standard $1,250, default $6,250; it can be cured by a certificate of correction filed within 60 days, after the tables are gone. Legalizing cellar seating means amending the Certificate of Occupancy: exits, ceiling height, ventilation, an accessible route.

violations.name: Step at the entrance with no accessible way in
violations.law: Americans with Disabilities Act, Title III, 42 U.S.C. §12182(b)(2)(A)(iv); NYC Administrative Code §8-107(4), §8-126
violations.note: Not a city inspection: a private lawsuit or a human rights complaint. NY1, 2019: a wave of suits against small NYC eateries, one over an eight-inch step, each asking up to $1,000 in damages plus attorney's fees and the fix itself. No public figure for a typical settlement was found; the lawyers' fees on both sides are usually the larger part. Federal filings under ADA Title III numbered 8,667 in 2025 (Seyfarth Shaw count). The NYC Human Rights Commission can add civil penalties of up to $125,000 (cited from memory). The $1,000 is the damages claim only.

violations.name: Music or equipment noise above the limit in a neighbor's home
violations.note: DEP's instruction sheet on commercial music violations (2023), read: the penalty under 24-231(a) can be mitigated from $2,000 to $0, for the first violation only and only if it rests on a reading taken in a person's residence; the owner must admit liability and have a noise consultant certify compliance within six weeks. An older DEP schedule (2009), read: one air-circulation device over 42 dB(A) or several over 45 dB(A) cost $560 for a first offense, $1,120 for a second, $1,680 for a third; those amounts may have changed.

violations.name: Licensed outdoor cafe set up against the rules
violations.note: Dining Out NYC enforcement page, read: for a first-time violation a licensed cafe receives a corrective action request with 30 days to fix it before any summons; after that, breaking the operation or design rules costs $200 for the first offense and $500 for the second and later ones, and repeat offenders can have the license suspended or revoked and the cafe removed. The engine should give one free month before charging. Game formula: $200, then $500.

officials.name: Health inspector
officials.agency: NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (DOHMH)
officials.realProcess: Unannounced, at least once a year. The inspector walks the whole shop with a thermometer and a flashlight, counts the seats, checks the restroom, the hand sinks, the lighting and the vents, and scores each violation in points: under 14 is an A. Fines are decided afterwards at a city hearing (OATH).
officials.note: Same id as in the pack: three D02 violations added to the checks, the rest unchanged.

officials.name: Water, sewer and noise inspector
officials.realProcess: DEP inspectors open the grease interceptor and ask for cleaning records, track which businesses have not filed the yearly backflow test, and answer 311 noise complaints by taking a sound reading inside the neighbor's apartment.
officials.note: Same id as in the pack: backflow and noise added.

officials.name: Buildings inspector
officials.realProcess: Comes after a 311 complaint, compares what he sees with the Certificate of Occupancy and the permits on file, and writes a summons to a city hearing (OATH). Immediately hazardous conditions cannot be cured by paperwork.

officials.name: Fire inspector
officials.agency: Fire Department of the City of New York (FDNY)
officials.realProcess: Walks the exits, checks that the path to every door is clear, looks at the extinguisher tags and, in rooms for 75 or more people, the Place of Assembly permit and the posted capacity. Violations go to a city hearing (OATH).

officials.name: Sanitation enforcement agent
officials.realProcess: Patrols the block and answers 311 complaints about blocked sidewalks. Anything a business leaves in the walking path can be ticketed on the spot: signs, benches, crates, planters.

officials.name: Human rights investigator
officials.realProcess: Acts on a complaint from a person who could not get in or be served. In real life most cases never reach the Commission: a private lawyer files in federal court and the owner settles and fixes the entrance.

officials.name: Outdoor dining inspector
officials.agency: NYC Department of Transportation (Dining Out NYC)
officials.realProcess: Inspectors patrol and answer 311 complaints. A licensed cafe with a setup problem first gets a corrective action request and 30 days to correct it; an unlicensed one is fined at once ($500, then $1,000) and can be ordered to clear the sidewalk.
officials.note: Same id as in the pack: one D02 violation added to the checks.

reports.name: Report a cafe with no customer restroom (311)
reports.text: In real life: a 311 complaint to the Health Department. An inspector counts the seats; with 20 or more there must be a supplied toilet for customers. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report an overcrowded room or blocked exit (311)
reports.text: In real life: a 311 complaint sent to the Buildings and Fire Departments. Inspectors compare the crowd with the Certificate of Occupancy, walk the exits and look into the cellar. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report a sign without a permit (311)
reports.text: In real life: a 311 complaint to the Buildings Department, which may be anonymous. In 2018 such calls tripled and left hundreds of shops with $6,000 fines. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report a blocked sidewalk or outdoor tables over the line (311)
reports.text: In real life: a 311 complaint about signs, benches, goods or cafe tables in the walking path. Sanitation enforcement tickets obstructions; the Transportation Department measures outdoor cafes against their plans. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report an entrance a wheelchair user cannot use
reports.text: In real life: a complaint to the NYC Commission on Human Rights, or a lawsuit. If there is a step and no ramp, bell or other way in, the owner pays damages and legal fees and still has to fix it. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report loud music or equipment (311)
reports.text: In real life: a 311 noise complaint. A DEP inspector takes a reading inside the neighbor's apartment; music over 42 decibels there is a violation. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

events.name: Wave of sign complaints on the avenue
events.text: Someone is calling 311 about every storefront sign on the strip. Buildings inspectors have to answer each call.
events.note: Real case: 1,046 illegal-sign complaints in 2018 against 310 in all of 2017, concentrated in southern Brooklyn (Buildings Department figures quoted by a local paper). The multiplier is a game value.

events.name: Water and sewer rates go up on July 1
events.text: The Water Board raises rates every July. Ice, espresso, dishwashing and the restroom all run through the meter.
events.note: Water Board rate schedule effective July 1, 2026, read: metered water $5.35 per 100 cubic feet (it was $5.05 the year before: +5.9%), wastewater 159% of the water charge, so $13.86 combined; minimum charge $0.49 a day. Water is roughly a seventh of the pack's utilities line by my estimate (about 12 hundred-cubic-feet a month = $166 of $1,100): 5.9% x 15% = about 1%. The rates are verified; the cafe's water use is the estimate.

ruleCards.title: Seat 20 needs a toilet
ruleCards.text: A cafe with 20 or more seats, outdoor ones included, must give customers a toilet they can reach without crossing the kitchen or storage. No toilet: $300 and 10 points at every inspection. Premises with a food permit by December 5, 1977 are exempt until they renovate.

ruleCards.title: A stocked restroom
ruleCards.text: A restroom without toilet paper, a waste bin or a self-closing door costs $200 and 2 to 5 points at inspection. A one-person restroom must also carry an all-gender sign on the wall next to the door (Local Law 79 of 2016).

ruleCards.title: The 75-person line
ruleCards.text: A room for fewer than 75 people, staff included, is business space and one exit can serve up to 74. At 75 it is a place of assembly: second exit, outward-swinging doors, a Buildings certificate and a yearly Fire Department permit. People are counted, not chairs.

ruleCards.title: How the code counts people
ruleCards.text: The building code counts one person per 15 sq ft where there are tables and chairs and one per 5 sq ft where people stand. A 70 sq ft queue area counts as 14 people, so a crowded line can take a room over its limit before the seats do.

ruleCards.title: Over capacity
ruleCards.text: More people inside than the Certificate of Occupancy allows is an immediately hazardous violation: $2,500, or $12,500 if you miss the hearing, and it cannot be cured with paperwork. For one big night, a temporary permit costs $250, filed 10 business days ahead.

ruleCards.title: The cellar is storage
ruleCards.text: A cellar listed as storage on the Certificate of Occupancy may hold stock, not customers. Seating down there is "occupancy contrary to the Certificate": $1,250, or $6,250 on default. Making it legal means exits, ceiling height and an amended certificate.

ruleCards.title: One step at the door
ruleCards.text: Federal law asks an existing business to remove barriers where readily achievable. A step with no ramp or bell invites a lawsuit: up to $1,000 in damages, the other side's legal fees and the fix. Federal courts took 8,667 disability-access suits in 2025, websites included.

ruleCards.title: Access inside the room
ruleCards.text: At least 5% of your seats must be usable from a wheelchair: a table 28 to 34 inches high with 27 inches of knee room, reached by a route at least 36 inches wide. Moving two chairs is free; a lawsuit over a blocked aisle is not.

ruleCards.title: The government shares the cost of access
ruleCards.text: A business with sales of $1 million or less, or no more than 30 full-time workers, gets a federal credit for ramps, doors and restroom changes: 50% of what it spends between $250 and $10,250 a year, up to $5,000 (IRS Form 8826).

ruleCards.title: Signs get reported
ruleCards.text: A wall sign over 6 sq ft needs a Buildings permit; a sign painted on the wall needs none. Work without a permit: $1,250, or $6,250 if you miss the hearing. In 2018 anonymous 311 complaints about signs tripled to over 1,000 before the Council froze the fines.

ruleCards.title: What an awning may say
ruleCards.text: An awning is a permitted job, and zoning limits its text: the shop's name and address, letters no taller than 12 inches, no more than 12 sq ft of lettering. Photos, menus and phone numbers printed on the fabric are what inspectors cite.

ruleCards.title: Landmark blocks
ruleCards.text: In a historic district any change to the outside of a storefront needs a Landmarks permit first: storefront, sign, awning, lighting, a new paint color, even a sidewalk cafe. Check the address on the Landmarks map before you sign the lease.

ruleCards.title: Roll-down gates
ruleCards.text: A 2009 law told shops to have gates at least 70% see-through by July 1, 2026; owners were quoted $6,000 to $7,000 a gate. The Council dropped the deadline 51-0 on June 30, 2026. The 70% rule now applies only to a new or replaced gate.

ruleCards.title: Your sign on their sidewalk
ruleCards.text: An A-frame sign may stand no more than 3 feet out from your wall and no taller than 5 feet. Beyond that, signs, benches and crates are sidewalk obstructions: $50 the first time, $100 each time after, $300 if you ignore the ticket.

ruleCards.title: How much sidewalk you can use
ruleCards.text: A sidewalk cafe must leave walkers half the sidewalk or 8 feet, whichever is more (10 feet on regional corridors, 12 on global ones), and stay 15 feet from a subway stair. On a 12-foot side-street sidewalk that leaves one row of small tables at most.

ruleCards.title: What outdoor seats cost
ruleCards.text: License $1,050 for four years; refundable deposit $1,500 (sidewalk) or $2,500 (roadway); roadway hearing notice $500-$900; then $6 to $31 per sq ft a year by sector. The city's own example: 120 sq ft of sidewalk costs $720 a year in most of the city, $3,720 in central Manhattan.

ruleCards.title: Roadway cafes all year
ruleCards.text: A seasonal roadway cafe runs April 1 to November 29 and must be gone by November 30. Since a 2026 law a year-round roadway license exists, at the higher sidewalk rates ($6-$31 per sq ft a year instead of $5-$25). Sidewalk cafes were always year-round.

ruleCards.title: Winter vestibules
ruleCards.text: A storm enclosure at the door is allowed only from November 15 through April 15, needs a permit and may stand no more than 18 inches beyond the building line. Left up after April 15, it is an illegal structure that anyone can report to 311.

ruleCards.title: Light is in the Health Code
ruleCards.text: The Health Code sets light levels: 50 foot-candles where food is prepared, 20 at hand sinks, dishwashing, inside fridges and in the restroom, 10 in dry storage. Bulbs over food must be shatterproof or shielded. Too dark: $100, waived the first time if you fix it.

ruleCards.title: The backflow test
ruleCards.text: The backflow device on the water line keeps cafe water out of the city main. Installing one costs $3,000-$5,000 in a small building (DEP's figures) and it must be tested every 12 months by a certified tester. Skip it and the city can fine you or disconnect your water.

ruleCards.title: 42 decibels upstairs
ruleCards.text: Music from a business may not exceed 42 decibels measured inside a neighbor's home; one rooftop fan or compressor has the same limit, several together 45. A first music violation is $2,000, reduced to $0 only if a noise consultant certifies the fix.

ruleCards.title: Sidewalk cellar doors
ruleCards.text: Sidewalk cellar doors may stand open during a delivery only while a person guards the opening. The city inspects doors that are bent, wobbly or left open and unprotected. A fall through an open hatch is a claim against whoever kept it.

ruleCards.title: No garbage disposal
ruleCards.text: Food waste grinders are not allowed in NYC businesses, and every business that sends grease down the drain should have a properly sized grease interceptor. Milk and coffee grounds go in the bin, not the sink.

ruleCards.title: Keep the way out clear
ruleCards.text: Every path to an exit must stay clear at all times. Milk crates in the back hallway or a chair in front of the rear door is a Fire Department summons: about $950 the first time and more than double for a repeat within 18 months.

ruleCards.title: Air you have to maintain
ruleCards.text: The Health Code requires working ventilation. Ventilation that is missing, badly installed or broken costs $200 and 2 to 5 points at inspection. Most leases make the tenant, not the landlord, pay for the air conditioning unit.

ruleCards.title: More than 30 people: two toilet rooms
ruleCards.text: Plumbing Code: where customers must be given a toilet and the space holds more than 30 people, staff included, it needs separate facilities. Two single all-gender rooms satisfy that. The rule bites when a space is built or altered, so seat 20 can mean two restrooms.

ruleCards.title: One door is not always enough
ruleCards.text: One exit serves a business room only if the farthest corner is within 75 feet of walking distance once more than 30 people use it (100 feet with sprinklers). A long, narrow storefront can need a second exit with 40 seats.

ruleCards.title: Open door, air conditioning on
ruleCards.text: Since 2015 NYC shops must shut doors and windows while the air conditioning runs. A food business with indoor seating whose door opens straight to the street is exempt; with a vestibule between door and seats it is not. The city made nearly 6,300 inspections in 2024.

ruleCards.title: Outdoor tables over the line
ruleCards.text: A licensed outdoor cafe that breaks the design or operating rules first gets a corrective action request and 30 days to fix it. After that: $200 for the first offense, $500 for each later one, and repeat offenders can lose the license.

ruleCards.title: Rules for the outdoor area
ruleCards.text: Outdoor seats count toward the 20-seat restroom line. You may not prepare or store food, utensils or equipment outside, nobody may smoke or vape there, and your pest control contract must be extended to cover the outdoor setup.

ruleCards.title: Candles need a permit
ruleCards.text: Candles on the tables need a Fire Department open flame permit in any restaurant, even one for fewer than 75 people: $210 a year. No lit candles where people stand, in an aisle or at an exit.

ruleCards.title: The unit on the roof has its own permit
ruleCards.text: An air conditioning or refrigeration unit mounted on the roof or hung from the ceiling needs a Fire Department permit: $105 per compressor, renewed every year. A small floor unit under five horsepower with ordinary refrigerant is exempt.

roadmap.title: Measure what is left for seats
roadmap.text: Before you sign, draw the room. Bar about 120 sq ft, line and pickup 70, accessible restroom 60, sinks and storage 120, door area 25: close to 400 sq ft that never holds a chair. In 800 sq ft that leaves room for about 22 seats; in 500 sq ft for six.

roadmap.title: Pick your seat count: 19 or 20 is a real decision
roadmap.text: With 20 or more seats, indoor and outdoor together, you must provide a customer restroom, and in a newly built or altered space for more than 30 people that means two toilet rooms. With 75 or more people the room becomes a place of assembly. Decide the count before the architect draws.
roadmap.agency: NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene

roadmap.title: Check the panel, the water line, the drain and the air conditioning
roadmap.text: Ask for the electrical panel size in amps: an espresso machine alone needs a 30-amp 220V circuit, and a service upgrade through Con Edison takes 3 to 6 months. Find the backflow device and the grease interceptor, and read in the lease who repairs the air conditioning unit.
roadmap.agency: Con Edison; NYC Department of Environmental Protection

roadmap.title: Look at the entrance the way a wheelchair user would
roadmap.text: A step at the door is the most common reason small NYC shops get sued. A compliant ramp needs one foot of length per inch of height; on an older building it may reach 44 inches onto the sidewalk with the Buildings Department's approval. A small business can claim back half the cost, up to $5,000 a year (IRS Form 8826).
roadmap.agency: NYC Department of Buildings; NYC Department of Transportation

roadmap.title: Find out if the block is landmarked before you design the front
roadmap.text: In a historic district every outside change needs a Landmarks permit before the Buildings Department will act: sign, awning, lighting, a new paint color. Outside one, a wall sign over 6 sq ft still needs a permit; a sign painted directly on the wall does not.

roadmap.title: Optional: apply for a roadway cafe
roadmap.text: A roadway cafe license is $1,050 for four years plus a refundable $2,500 deposit, a hearing notice of $500-$900 and a yearly fee per square foot. The program says review can take six months. A year-round license costs more per square foot than a seasonal one, and the structure itself runs $5,000 to $35,000.
roadmap.agency: NYC Department of Transportation (Dining Out NYC)

suppliers.what: A commercial HVAC company for a quarterly service contract and for the day the unit fails
suppliers.whereToFind: Ask the landlord who installed the unit and ask neighboring restaurants who services theirs; get three bids that list visits, filters and labor rates
suppliers.note: No directory was checked; the advice follows vendor guides on service contracts.

suppliers.what: A licensed sign hanger who files the Buildings permit, makes the sign or awning and installs it; many also build seasonal vestibules
suppliers.whereToFind: The Buildings Department license search lists licensed sign hangers; sign shops in your borough quote the permit together with the sign
suppliers.note: The Buildings Department page says larger signs need a permit obtained by a licensed sign hanger (already cited in the pack).

suppliers.category: Licensed master plumber and backflow tester
suppliers.what: Installs the grease interceptor and the backflow device, files with the city, and tests the backflow device every year
suppliers.whereToFind: The Buildings Department license search for master plumbers; DEP keeps a list of certified backflow testers
suppliers.note: DEP requires a certified tester for the yearly test; the tester list itself was not opened.

suppliers.what: An architect or accessibility consultant who walks the entrance, the route to the counter and the restroom and lists the cheapest fixes
suppliers.whereToFind: The Buildings Department publishes a storefront accessibility guide; the Mayor's Office for People with Disabilities and NYC Small Business Services answer questions for free
suppliers.note: The Buildings Department presentation on storefront accessibility was found by search; the free advice offices are named from general knowledge and were not checked.

suppliers.what: A glazier with 24-hour board-up service and a gate company for roll-down grilles
suppliers.whereToFind: Ask the landlord and the neighbors; keep the glazier's number at the register, because a broken window has to be boarded the same night
suppliers.note: Gate prices from 2026 press reports ($6,000-$7,000 for one gate); glass prices from glazier guides outside NYC.

seatThresholds.rule: A customer toilet is required at a seating capacity of 20 or more, indoor and outdoor seats and shared seating counted together; premises that held a food permit on or before December 5, 1977 are exempt until a renovation that needs a Buildings construction permit
seatThresholds.penalty: Code 5E, critical: $300 and 10 points at each inspection ($350 and 28 points at the worst level)

seatThresholds.rule: Where customers must be given a toilet and the space holds more than 30 people, staff included, separate facilities are required; two single all-gender toilet rooms satisfy it. Applies when a space is built or altered
seatThresholds.note: Read in the 2022 Plumbing Code. No setupItemId on purpose: the engine should not block on it until the lead decides whether a second room is a separate item. A 20-seat room is over 30 people by the code's count (20 x 18 / 15 = 24, + 3 staff, + a queue).

seatThresholds.rule: 75 or more people, staff included (the occupant load, not chairs) make the room a place of assembly: Place of Assembly Certificate of Operation, yearly Fire Department permit, a second exit, outward-swinging doors. Below 75 one exit may serve up to 74
seatThresholds.law: NYC Building Code Table 1004.1.3, Table 1006.2.1, §1010.1.2.2; NYC Administrative Code §28-117.1
seatThresholds.note: Corrects the pack's entry, which read the line as 75 seats. The law counts people: seating area / 15 sq ft + standing area / 5 sq ft + staff (all read in the 2022 Building Code). 48 seats is my conversion for a room laid out at 18 sq ft a seat with a 70 sq ft queue and 3 staff: 48 x 18 / 15 = 58, + 14 + 3 = 75. The pack's maximum of 40 seats stays under it; a standing event does not. The threshold number is verified, the seat conversion is an estimate.

floorPlan.note: Where the floor goes in a counter-service cafe. The fixed core barely changes with the size of the space, which is why small rooms lose a far larger share to it than the engine's flat 60% assumes. All zone sizes are my estimates from the cited rules of thumb; none is a legal minimum except where said.

zones.basis: About 16 ft of counter x 7.5 ft deep (front counter, work aisle, back counter). Guides ask for at least 8 linear feet of counter; a Russian guide gives 2-3 m of bar and no more than three steps per drink.
Ten people at about 7 sq ft each; the Building Code counts 5 net sq ft per standing person when it computes occupancy (Table 1004.1.3, read).

Accessible single-user room: 35 sq ft in the Access Board's smallest sample plan (7 ft x 5 ft, search excerpt), about 48 typical, plus the door approach; the Access Board itself says the standards set no minimum room size (read). An employee toilet is required at any size (Health Code 81.22(a), read). A second room is needed in a new or altered space for more than 30 people with 20 or more seats.
15% of 800 sq ft: three-compartment sink, hand sink, mop sink, water heater, dry storage, trash and recycling bins. Guides give 15%-25% for the back of house.
Door swing and the 5 ft x 5 ft a wheelchair needs to turn inside the door.

seatsBySpace.comment: To-go only; three window stools if storage goes to the cellar

floorPlan.formula: seats = floor((sqft - fixedCoreSqft) / netSqftPerSeat); seatsEngineToday = min(40, floor(sqft x 0.6 / 18))

outdoorSqftPerChair.note: NYC Open Data, old sidewalk cafe license records (dataset qcdj-rwhu), queried: 324 licenses with both figures, 92,391 sq ft and 8,072 chairs in total = 11.4 sq ft per chair; the average licensed cafe had 285 sq ft and 25 chairs. Pre-2024 program, both enclosed and unenclosed cafes.

eventCatalog.name: No free table
eventCatalog.text: People walk in, look for a seat, find none and leave without ordering.
eventCatalog.trigger: state: seated orders above 85% of what the seats can turn in the month
eventCatalog.realSignal: Your own seat utilization: seated orders divided by seat capacity
eventCatalog.realFrequency: An owner's account on NPR (2014): "We saw a lot of customers come in, look for a table, not find one and leave. It was money flowing out the door for us."
eventCatalog.note: The 5% loss is a game value on top of the orders the engine already drops for lack of seats: it stands for people who would have taken their order to go but left when they saw a packed room.

eventCatalog.name: The room turns into an office
eventCatalog.text: Remote workers hold half the tables from nine to five on one coffee each.
eventCatalog.trigger: state: laptop policy 'open' and seat utilization above 70%
eventCatalog.realSignal: Devices on your guest Wi-Fi for more than 90 minutes at 11am
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Bloom Intelligence, Wi-Fi presence at 25 US coffee shops, June-September 2026: 32 minutes on site for a one-time visitor, nearly two hours for the most frequent visitors
eventCatalog.note: The cold-month list is my assumption (people who would work in a park come indoors); the 15% loss of turns is half of what the 'peak_limits' laptop policy wins back.

eventCatalog.name: One person, four chairs
eventCatalog.text: Every four-top has one guest, a laptop and a coat on it. The room is a third occupied and completely full.
eventCatalog.trigger: state: layout without a communal table or bar seats, parties of one at peak
eventCatalog.realSignal: Count at 9am: tables in use against chairs in use
eventCatalog.realFrequency: A roaster-cafe chief executive quoted in the press: someone working alone usually takes up two to four seats, and a $6 drink buys about 90 minutes
eventCatalog.note: 0.75 = chairs really used when half the tables for two hold one guest. The quote was seen in a search excerpt of a syndicated article, not in the original interview.

eventCatalog.name: "We sat in a stranger's lap"
eventCatalog.text: Reviews start to mention elbows, bags and overheard phone calls.
eventCatalog.trigger: decision: seating layout 'tight' for two months or more
eventCatalog.realSignal: Share of new reviews that mention space or noise
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Cornell field study (2009): guests at tables 20 inches or less apart rated almost everything lower and were significantly less likely to return
eventCatalog.note: The study was a fine-dining dinner room, one restaurant; the size of the effect for a coffee shop is a game value.

eventCatalog.name: Dead room at 3pm
eventCatalog.text: Forty chairs, four guests. The shop looks closed from the street.
eventCatalog.trigger: state: seat utilization under 30% for the month
eventCatalog.realSignal: Your own seat utilization
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Survey research (2025) finds a crowded restaurant works as social proof and lifts guests' pleasure; other marketing research finds the opposite for status goods. For coffee the effect is unproven.
eventCatalog.note: Deliberately small. The honest move for an oversized room is the opposite of the crowded one: invite the laptops, or take chairs out and make it a lounge.

eventCatalog.name: The line reaches the door
eventCatalog.text: At 8:30 the queue runs to the entrance. People on the sidewalk look in and keep walking.
eventCatalog.trigger: state: peak-hour orders above what the bar can make
eventCatalog.realSignal: People visible in line from the door at the morning peak
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Management Science (2013), supermarket deli data: buyers react to the length of the line, not to its speed; the working paper equates a moderately longer line with a 5% price increase. A 2024 survey of 1,202 US adults: 70% will wait at most 15 minutes in a physical line and 61% have left one.
eventCatalog.note: 5% taken from the working paper's price equivalence with the pack's price elasticity of -1.3 in mind (5% x 1.3 = 6.5%, rounded down). The deli is not a cafe; treat as an order of magnitude.

eventCatalog.name: Phone orders bury the bar
eventCatalog.text: Twenty tickets print at 8:15. The people standing in front of you wait while cups for people who are not here yet line the counter.
eventCatalog.trigger: decision: order-ahead switched on with the bar at minimum staff
eventCatalog.realSignal: Share of orders placed by phone at peak; minutes from order to handoff
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Starbucks, spring 2024: more than 3 in 10 drink orders came through the app and a mid-teens percent of mobile orders went uncompleted; a research firm found 8% of its customers waited 15 to 30 minutes. The fix it chose: a separate pickup area and a four-minute target.
eventCatalog.note: A chain's numbers, used as the direction of the effect; the 5% capacity loss matches the lever.

eventCatalog.name: Your line is on the neighbors' stoop
eventCatalog.text: The weekend queue runs past three buildings. Residents call 311 about a blocked sidewalk and the landlord gets letters.
eventCatalog.trigger: state: reputation above 0.85 and weekend demand above capacity for two months
eventCatalog.realSignal: 311 complaints of a blocked sidewalk at your address
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Local press, Brooklyn, 2024: a bakery's weekend line of 20 minutes and more spilled across neighbors' stoops; in Manhattan residents describe lines of about a hundred people blocking a sidewalk several days a week

eventCatalog.name: The inspector counts chairs
eventCatalog.text: Stools at the window, the bench, the two tables outside: everything counts toward 20.

eventCatalog.realSignal: Health Department inspection (at least once a year, sooner after a complaint)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Health Code 81.22(b); NYC Health: 20 or more seats, including both indoor and outdoor seats; NYC311 adds seating shared by several food businesses in a common space
eventCatalog.note: Not a random event: the inspection finds what is there. 10 points and $300 each time (Chapter 23, code 5E).

eventCatalog.name: Accessibility suits reach your avenue
eventCatalog.text: A law firm is filing suits against every shop on the strip with a step at the door. Papers arrive next month.
eventCatalog.trigger: announced one month ahead; hits every business that still has the barrier

eventCatalog.realFrequency: NY1 (2019): a surge of suits by a small group of plaintiffs against small NYC businesses; a law review article (2023) describes one lawyer filing dozens of near-identical suits, among them one in 2015 over a step with no ramp; The Guardian (2025) reports an East Village cafe owner served with a suit listing 35 violations
eventCatalog.note: The game should announce it, so the month before is the player's chance to fix the door. Real cases named in the sources are evidence only.

eventCatalog.name: Somebody is reporting every sign on the strip
eventCatalog.text: Anonymous 311 calls about storefront signs triple. Buildings inspectors must answer each one.

eventCatalog.note: Mirrors the standard event of the same name in 'events'. Today's penalty for work without a permit is $1,250 standard and $6,250 on default (Buildings schedule, read).

eventCatalog.name: The roll-down gate deadline
eventCatalog.text: The city says every solid security gate must be replaced with a see-through one by July 1. Quotes run $6,000 to $7,000 a gate.
eventCatalog.trigger: announced in February; on June 30 the Council cancels the deadline

The lesson is real: read deadlines, but watch the Council calendar. The new rule (70% see-through only when a gate is installed or replaced) stays.

eventCatalog.name: Cold blast at every door swing

eventCatalog.realFrequency: DEP (search excerpt): about 60% of the city's sewers carry storm water and sewage in one pipe and back up into buildings when rain overwhelms them. Two closed days are my estimate (a contractor's story has a restaurant back in four days after three feet of water). Sewer backup is normally not covered without a separate insurance endorsement. mechanics.title: The floor is a budget: a fixed core, then seats
mechanics.playerDecision: Which address to take and how to spend its floor: bar length, storage upstairs or in the cellar, a customer restroom or 19 seats, comfortable or tight tables.
mechanics.engineMath: Replace maxSizeFor = floor(sqft x 0.6 / sqftPerUnit) with floor((sqft - fixedCoreSqft) / netSqftPerSeat x seatsFitMult). fixedCoreSqft is 395 (335 with cellar storage); netSqftPerSeat is 18, or 15 / 22 by the seating_layout lever. The flat 60% overstates small rooms (400 sq ft: 13 seats today, none in reality) and understates large ones. Until the engine changes, sizing.sqftPerUnit = 21 makes the two formulas agree at 800 sq ft.

mechanics.title: Chairs are not seats: tables fill before chairs do
mechanics.playerDecision: The mix of two-tops, four-tops, communal table and bar stools.
mechanics.engineMath: effectiveSeats = seats x tableUse, where tableUse is 0.75 for a room of two- and four-tops and 0.9 with a communal table and a window bar (lever seating_layout). Utilization, the crowding penalty and lost seated orders are computed against effectiveSeats. One wheelchair-usable place per 20 seats (5%) must stay free of fixed stools.

mechanics.title: Crowded and empty are slopes, not switches
mechanics.playerDecision: Seat count against demand, month by month: add or remove chairs, change the layout, send people outside.
mechanics.engineMath: Today: one flag above crowdPenaltyAbove (-0.08 quality) and one below emptyPenaltyBelow (-0.1 reputation target). Proposed: u = seated orders / seat capacity. Walk-outs (people who see no table and leave without ordering) = 0 below u = 0.7, rising linearly to 5% of all demand at u = 0.85 and 12% at u = 1.0. Quality loss rises from 0 at 0.7 to 0.08 at 1.0. The empty-room penalty starts below u = 0.3 and is at most -0.03 reputation, because 60% of buyers never look for a seat. All four numbers are game values anchored to the cited studies, not measurements.

mechanics.title: The line people see decides whether they join it
mechanics.playerDecision: Queue layout, a pickup shelf, order-ahead, a second pair of hands at the peak.
mechanics.engineMath: The month hides the rush, so compute one peak hour a day: arrivals = daily orders x peakHourShare; made = baristas on the bar x drinks per barista-hour. The backlog is the visible line. While the line fits the queue zone (queueSqft / 7 people) nobody is lost; each further 5 people in view costs 5% of that hour's arrivals (the deli study's price equivalence applied through the pack's elasticity). A line past the door adds the sidewalk problem. Lever queue_setup hides part of the line (waiting moves to the pickup shelf) and order-ahead removes people from the line but adds their drinks to the bar.

mechanics.title: Who sits how long: the stay-length mix sets what a seat earns
mechanics.playerDecision: Laptop and Wi-Fi policy, music, seat comfort, outlets.
mechanics.engineMath: unitsServedPerSizeMonth = openHours x 60 x meanOccupancy / meanStayMinutes x 30. With 12 hours, 47% occupancy and a mean stay of 60 minutes (70% of seated guests x 35 min + 30% x 120 min) this gives 170. Levers change the mix through seatTurnsMult: laptop_policy peak_limits 1.2, no_wifi 1.4; music calm 0.9, upbeat 1.1; lounge seating 0.85; communal 1.15. Multiply them, cap the product at 1.6. Each restrictive option also takes a slice of demand (its 'effects.demand').

mechanics.title: Three lines in the law: seat 20, person 31 and person 75
mechanics.playerDecision: Stop at 19 seats, or pay for a customer restroom; keep events under 75 people, or buy a temporary permit, or become a place of assembly.
mechanics.engineMath: Seats for the 20 line = indoor + outdoor seats (extra.seatThresholds[0]; the engine already blocks a resize without the item). People = seatingSqft / 15 + standingSqft / 5 + staff on shift. Over 30 people in a room that must give customers a toilet: two toilet rooms when the space is built or altered (120 sq ft instead of 60). 75 or more: place of assembly; it matters only for events or rooms above about 48 seats. One exit also requires that the farthest corner be within 75 feet of travel once more than 30 people use the room (100 feet with sprinklers): a place attribute for long, narrow storefronts. A resize that crosses 20 takes 60 to 120 sq ft out of the seating area, which is why the step from 19 to 20 seats can leave fewer seats than before.

mechanics.title: Outdoor seats: geometry, license, season
mechanics.playerDecision: Apply for a sidewalk or roadway cafe (and wait), run tables without a license (existing shortcut), or do without.
mechanics.engineMath: Whether the address can have a sidewalk cafe at all is geometry: cafeDepth = sidewalkWidth - clearPath - curbZone, with clearPath = the greater of half the sidewalk width or 8 ft (10 ft on regional corridors, 12 ft on global corridors); 15 ft from a subway stair, 10 ft and 5 ft from listed street objects, 8 ft of clear path past tree beds, street lights and hydrants. outdoorSeats = floor(cafeSqft / 11.4). Yearly fee = cafeSqft x sector rate (sidewalk and year-round roadway $6 / $10 / $18 / $31; seasonal roadway $5 / $8 / $14 / $25; the two dearest sectors are Manhattan at or below 125th Street). Seats are usable in monthsActive and count toward the 20-seat line. The license arrives after waitDays (program: up to six months). A licensed cafe that breaks the rules gets 30 days, then $200 and $500.
