nonObvious.text: The 75 line that turns a cafe into a place of assembly counts people, not chairs, staff included, and the code counts a standing person at 5 sq ft: a 70 sq ft queue area is 14 people on paper.
nonObvious.why: An owner who thinks '75 seats, never my problem' can cross the line with 48 seats, or with one standing-room event: $2,500, no cure.

nonObvious.text: Seat number 20 is the most expensive chair in the shop: it brings the duty to give customers a toilet, 10 inspection points without one, and in a newly built or altered space for more than 30 people it means two toilet rooms. Outdoor seats count toward it.
nonObvious.why: Two sidewalk tables can turn a legal 18-seat room into a violation.

nonObvious.text: A premises that held a food permit on or before December 5, 1977 is exempt from the customer-toilet rule, and loses the exemption the day it does a renovation that needs a Buildings permit.
nonObvious.why: Taking over an old luncheonette as-is can be legal with 30 seats and no customer restroom; renovating it is what triggers the restroom.

nonObvious.text: A shared staff-and-customer toilet is legal only if customers do not walk through the kitchen, prep, storage or dishwashing area to reach it.
nonObvious.why: The position of one door decides whether the existing toilet counts.

nonObvious.text: About 400 sq ft of any cafe never holds a chair: bar, line, restroom, sinks and storage, door. A 500 sq ft space has room for about six seats, not the sixteen a flat '60% is seating' rule suggests.
nonObvious.why: Rent is paid on all 500.

nonObvious.text: One guest with a laptop takes two to four seats, so a room of two- and four-tops is full when well under half its chairs are occupied.
nonObvious.why: The owner counts 20 seats; the customer at the door sees no free table.

nonObvious.text: A bakery cafe that switched off Wi-Fi and banned screens at lunch saw sales go up, not down: people had been coming in, finding no table and leaving.
nonObvious.why: The lost customers are invisible: they never reach the register.

nonObvious.text: Buyers react to how long a line looks, not to how fast it moves. Merging two short lines into one long fast one can lose sales.
nonObvious.why: Speeding the bar is not enough; where the waiting people stand matters.

nonObvious.text: Order-ahead can cut capacity instead of adding it: at Starbucks a mid-teens percent of mobile orders went uncompleted in spring 2024 because the bars were buried.
nonObvious.why: The app adds drinks to the same two hands at the same minute.

nonObvious.text: Guests at tables 20 inches or less apart leave sooner, which looks like better turnover, and are significantly less likely to come back.
nonObvious.why: The squeeze pays this month and costs next quarter.

nonObvious.text: Slow music lengthened restaurant stays from 57 to 80 minutes in a 2024 experiment and the bill did not change.
nonObvious.why: The playlist is a seat-turnover control that costs nothing.

nonObvious.text: The law against open doors with the air conditioning on covers every shop, but a food business with indoor seating whose door opens straight to the street is exempt. Add a vestibule between door and seats and the exemption is gone.
nonObvious.why: Owners copy each other: the cafe may prop its door, the boutique next door gets inspected (nearly 6,300 inspections in 2024). A permanent vestibule changes the cafe's own status.

nonObvious.text: Sign complaints can be anonymous 311 calls. In 2018 they tripled to more than a thousand and left small shops with fines for signs that had hung for years. A sign painted directly on the wall needs no permit at all.
nonObvious.why: A sign is the easiest thing for a rival or an angry neighbor to report: $1,250 today, $6,250 on default.

nonObvious.text: An awning may carry only the shop's name and address, in letters no taller than 12 inches and 12 sq ft in all. Menus, photos and phone numbers on the fabric are violations.
nonObvious.why: Most awning shops will print anything the owner asks for.

nonObvious.text: In 2026 a law from 2009 was about to force every shop to replace solid roll-down gates by July 1; owners were quoted $6,000-$7,000. The Council repealed the deadline on June 30, one day before.
nonObvious.why: Some owners paid in spring for something that was never required.

nonObvious.text: An A-frame sign is tolerated only within 3 feet of your own wall and under 5 feet tall. Past that it is a sidewalk obstruction like any crate.
nonObvious.why: Owners put the sign at the curb, where walkers see it; that is the illegal spot.

nonObvious.text: A winter vestibule is legal only from November 15 to April 15 and only 18 inches past the building line.
nonObvious.why: It costs $4,500 or more every season and has to be stored all summer.

nonObvious.text: Most small leases make the tenant repair and replace the air conditioning unit that serves the space. A dead unit is an $8,000-$40,000 bill in NYC.
nonObvious.why: New tenants assume the building's equipment is the landlord's.

nonObvious.text: A Con Edison electrical service upgrade takes 3 to 6 months by contractors' accounts. A space with too small a panel is months of rent away from running a second espresso machine.
nonObvious.why: Nobody checks the panel at the showing.

nonObvious.text: When the utility finds a leak anywhere in the building's gas piping it locks the whole building's gas, and the tenant waits for the landlord's plumber: six weeks in one 2025-2026 press case, four months in another.
nonObvious.why: A cafe that needs no gas at all is immune; that choice is made at build-out.

nonObvious.text: The backflow device on the water line must be tested by a certified tester every year; the city can disconnect the water of a business that does not, and installing one in a small building costs $3,000-$5,000 by the city's own figures.
nonObvious.why: It is a part most owners have never seen, behind a panel in the cellar.

nonObvious.text: Food waste grinders are banned in NYC businesses, and a coffee shop needs a grease interceptor even with no cooking.
nonObvious.why: Milk fat is grease to the sewer department.

nonObvious.text: The Health Code sets light levels: 50 foot-candles at the prep counter, 20 at the hand sink. A fashionably dark bar fails an inspection.
nonObvious.why: Designers light for mood, inspectors carry a meter.

nonObvious.text: Music is measured in the neighbor's bedroom, not in your room: 42 decibels there is the limit. A first violation is $2,000 and drops to $0 only if you prove the fix.
nonObvious.why: A ground-floor cafe under apartments shares a ceiling with its complainants.

nonObvious.text: About 60% of NYC sewers are combined; in a cloudburst they back up through cellar drains. Any food that touched that water must be thrown out, and ordinary insurance does not cover sewer backup without a separate endorsement.
nonObvious.why: The cellar is where a small cafe keeps its stock.

nonObvious.text: Sidewalk cellar doors may be open only while a person stands guard.
nonObvious.why: The morning delivery arrives during the rush, when nobody can leave the bar.

nonObvious.text: A sidewalk cafe must leave walkers the greater of half the sidewalk or 8 feet (10 on regional corridors, 12 on global ones). On an ordinary 12-15 foot side-street sidewalk that leaves room for one row of small tables or none.
nonObvious.why: Owners budget for outdoor seats before measuring the sidewalk.

nonObvious.text: A roadway cafe can easily cost more than $35,000 to set up. The yearly city fee is modest in most of the city ($800-$960 for 160 sq ft) and about five times that in central Manhattan; the new year-round license costs more per square foot than the seasonal one.
nonObvious.why: The pandemic-era free shed is gone; the structure, not the fee, is the real bill.

nonObvious.text: A $113 portable ramp does not make a 7-inch step compliant: the standard asks for a foot of ramp per inch of height, 36 inches of width and a 60-inch landing. On a building older than 1969 a permanent ramp may reach 44 inches onto the sidewalk with city approval.
nonObvious.why: The cheap fix shows good faith but is not the end of the exposure; half the cost of the real fix comes back as a tax credit, up to $5,000 a year.

nonObvious.text: A one-person restroom must have an all-gender sign on the wall next to the door.
nonObvious.why: 'Men' and 'Women' signs on single-occupant rooms have been illegal in NYC since 2017.

nonObvious.text: Since January 27, 2025 the largest coffee chain requires a purchase to use its restrooms. Under 20 seats an independent cafe owes the public nothing either, but it is the one people ask.
nonObvious.why: Restroom traffic is a cost line and a seat blocker nobody budgets.

nonObvious.text: A hit product can put a line across the neighbors' stoops, and then the complaints are about the sidewalk, not the coffee.
nonObvious.why: Success creates a new kind of inspection risk.

nonObvious.text: One big event needs its own permit: a Temporary Place of Assembly certificate is $250, filed at least 10 business days ahead, plus $100 for each day late.
nonObvious.why: The legal path is cheap; ignoring it is a $2,400 immediately hazardous violation.

nonObvious.text: The electric bill has a part that depends on your single highest half hour of the month. An oven that runs twenty minutes a day can raise the bill more than its energy use explains.
nonObvious.why: Owners compare kWh; larger commercial accounts are also billed on peak kW.

nonObvious.text: In a room that needs a second look by the plumbing code, the number is 30, not 20 or 75: above 30 people, staff included, a space that must give customers a toilet needs separate facilities, in practice two toilet rooms.
nonObvious.why: The Health Department asks for 'a toilet'; the architect drawing a permit set must show two, and they take 120 sq ft.

nonObvious.text: One exit is legal for up to 74 people only if the farthest corner is within 75 feet of walking distance (100 with sprinklers, or with 30 people or fewer). A deep, narrow storefront can need a rear exit long before it is crowded.
nonObvious.why: Typical NYC storefronts are 20 feet wide and 80 to 100 feet deep.

nonObvious.text: Candles on the tables need a Fire Department open flame permit in any restaurant, even a tiny one: $210 a year.
nonObvious.why: Nobody thinks of a tea light as something with a permit.

nonObvious.text: An air conditioning unit on the roof or hung from the ceiling needs its own Fire Department permit: $105 per compressor every year.
nonObvious.why: The unit came with the space; the permit did not.

nonObvious.text: Nothing may be stored or prepared in the outdoor dining area, nobody may smoke or vape there, and the pest control contract has to be extended to cover it.
nonObvious.why: Outdoor seats add rules as well as sales.

nonObvious.text: In a historic district even a new paint color on the storefront, and a sidewalk cafe, need a Landmarks permit.
nonObvious.why: The Landmarks permit comes before the Buildings permit, and the rent does not wait.

nonObvious.text: A licensed outdoor cafe gets one free warning: a corrective action request and 30 days. An unlicensed one is fined on the first visit, $500 and then $1,000.
nonObvious.why: The license is what buys the grace period.

nonObvious.text: The customer toilet may be one floor down, in the cellar, as far as the plumbing code goes, but the route may not pass through a kitchen or storage room and new work has to be accessible.
nonObvious.why: Many old NYC cafes send guests down a steep stair; a new build-out cannot copy that.

forOtherNiches.note: Found while checking the cafe and not usable in it: the open-door rule binds shops without indoor food seating. For the barbershop, the bodega and any retail niche this is a real violation; it belongs in _common or in those packs.

violations.name: Door or window open while the air conditioning runs
violations.note: DCWP inspection checklist (updated August 2022), read: stores must keep doors and windows shut when the air conditioning runs, whatever their size; allowed only for deliveries, an emergency, actively serving food or drinks to outdoor customers, or if the business sells food, has indoor seating and the door or window leads directly outside (not if a vestibule or foyer stands between). Chains with five or more NYC stores must post a sign. DCWP press release (April 2025), read: nearly 6,300 inspections in 2024, 89 violations for open doors and 267 for a missing sign. The $250 and $500 amounts are from 2015 press reports of the law and were not found in a current schedule.
